doc.title: Darius Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 29, 2024

title: Rehearsal approach and parallels with segregated America
summary: Rehearsing C Jam Blues style tunes, and Monk's observation that the Brubeck group broke segregation rules.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I just — I can almost I think picture your first few rehearsals. Because I’ve been in situations where you have both ends of what you’re describing and sometimes I would
say, “All right let’s do ‘C Jam Blues’ here’s what it sounds like. Get everybody to play something together to just get some motion going.

Yeah. Right. Well then in that case if there was any resistance it would be to reading it at all. You know. But if you said after three choruses, okay, let’s see, how would I work through that — “Okay, head twice — there’s been a lot of brass let’s have a guitar or a piano solo, first trombone set a riff.” You know? And then —

Well I’m going to move on but I just wanted to make a comment that your description of the Brubeck group in the late ‘70s when you went there, it’s so ironic because I’ve spoken to many elderly musicians who went through that over here — traveling in the south, segregated audiences, no white or black musicians on the stage at the same time, and what you’re describing just — I don’t have a question here, it’s just an observation that is worth noting.

Yeah. Well we, you know as I said, we broke those rules, we were an exception, the rules were not abrogated as a result but we just didn’t play the game by their rules. And, you know, obviously we’re proud of that and obviously that impacted on what my work would be later.
